purpose: A further 12 original articles covering heritage and ecology across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Pacific; World Heritage, Tentative, Ramsar and museum status explicitly distinguished.
rights: Original research writing, cited factual sources, no cleared photos.
preservation: Country editorial only; shop and profile balances untouched.

sections.title: An old city in Khorezm
sections.body: Kunya-Urgench lies in northern Turkmenistan, close to the Amu Darya river region. Its surviving monuments reveal the importance of Khorezm as a centre of trade, learning and political influence at different periods. Much of the old urban fabric has disappeared, leaving buildings that must be interpreted within a broader historic landscape rather than imagined as a complete, uninterrupted medieval city.

sections.title: Architecture built through time
sections.body: The protected monuments include mausoleums, a tall minaret and remnants of religious and civic buildings. Their designs show skilled brickwork and decoration connected with architectural traditions across Central Asia. Not every structure dates to the same century, and later restoration has changed how some are presented. The site provides material clues to shifting artistic influences and forms of patronage.

sections.title: A crossroads of routes
sections.body: Historical networks across the region linked oasis settlements, river routes and wider trade connections. Environmental and political changes affected the fortunes of urban centres. Kunya-Urgench should therefore be seen as part of the history of the whole region, not as an isolated monument in the desert. Archaeological work helps reconstruct uses of space that are no longer obvious on the ground.

sections.title: Protecting remains in a changing landscape
sections.body: Conservation involves care for exposed masonry, visitor paths and neighbouring land use. Researchers and heritage specialists must distinguish original materials from repairs. The site shows how architecture, river geography and commerce helped build a major historic centre, while demonstrating the difficulty of preserving monuments when much of their original urban setting has changed.

records.hook: North Korea — Complex of Koguryo Tombs

sections.title: A collection of ancient burial places
sections.body: The Complex of Koguryo Tombs lies in parts of the northern Korean Peninsula, with groups of burial chambers located in several areas. The tombs date from the historical Koguryo kingdom, whose territories extended across parts of the peninsula and neighbouring northeast Asia. Their location and construction offer evidence of elite burial practices within a wider regional cultural history.

sections.title: Paintings that preserve everyday details
sections.body: Some chambers contain remarkable wall paintings showing figures, clothing, animals and scenes associated with beliefs and social life. These images are particularly valuable because relatively few surviving tombs retain such paintings. Interpretations rely on archaeology and the comparison of imagery; they cannot reveal the thoughts of every person who lived during the period. Tomb art is a selective cultural record.

sections.title: Engineering below earthen mounds
sections.body: Stone chambers, supporting structures and the construction of ceilings required skilled work. Burial mounds were placed within landscapes that could carry religious or symbolic meanings, although the evidence varies from one location to another. Damage from past disturbance has reduced some archaeological information. The sites are a serial group rather than one massive burial mound.

sections.title: Conserving vulnerable interiors
sections.body: Changes in moisture, temperature and biological growth can harm surviving paintings. Archaeological conservation therefore demands controlled access and long-term monitoring. The Koguryo tombs offer insight into historic Korean culture and its wider connections, showing why fragile artwork can be as important to understanding a society as more monumental remains above ground.

sections.title: A plateau above the Dead Sea
sections.body: Masada occupies a high, isolated plateau overlooking the Dead Sea region. Its steep sides offered strong natural protection, and buildings were constructed on the summit under Herod the Great. Remains include palatial spaces, storage areas and water installations. The location is essential to understanding the archaeology: the hilltop created both defensive advantages and major practical problems for permanent occupation.

sections.title: Water management in an arid setting
sections.body: Engineers built systems for collecting and storing runoff so people could use water despite the dry climate. Cisterns, channels and terraces provide evidence of planning and technical skill. The surviving works are valuable for understanding how a large complex functioned rather than seeing Masada solely through stories about its final siege.

sections.title: Historical memory and archaeological evidence
sections.body: The site is closely associated with the Roman siege during the first century CE. Roman camps, fortifications and a siege ramp remain in the surrounding landscape. Written accounts and material evidence need to be evaluated separately because interpretations of the final events have been debated. This history has acquired strong symbolic meaning, but scholarship should still acknowledge uncertainty.

sections.title: A large landscape of surviving remains
sections.body: Protecting the summit alone would overlook the Roman works around it and the dramatic desert setting. Conservation involves delicate stonework, visitor management and exposure to severe weather. Masada provides an opportunity to consider historical interpretation, the engineering of water supply and the interaction between a natural landform and successive human uses.

sections.title: A low island in the Gulf
sections.body: Failaka Island lies offshore from Kuwait, where the sea connects the island with the coast and wider Gulf waterways. Archaeological remains testify to occupation across many periods. The island is included on Kuwait's UNESCO Tentative List and has not been inscribed as a World Heritage site. Its significance involves the accumulation of different settlements rather than one single ancient city.

sections.title: Maritime routes and cultural contacts
sections.body: Location was central to Failaka's history. Communities could connect with mainland settlements and trading networks, while access to water and suitable landing places influenced settlement choices. Archaeologists have identified evidence from several cultural periods, including ancient Gulf and Hellenistic connections. Different buildings and objects must be interpreted according to their dates rather than grouped under one civilisation.

sections.title: Layers of architecture and settlement
sections.body: Structures, artefacts and buried remains reveal how human activity changed across time. Some areas carry more recent histories as well, meaning the archaeology cannot be separated from modern experiences on the island. Documenting the exact position and context of finds is important because excavating without careful records could destroy valuable information about the sequence of occupations.

sections.title: Conserving the whole island
sections.body: Coastal erosion, development and other activities create challenges for site protection. Heritage management must consider residents, access and the wider coastal landscape along with important excavated areas. Failaka illustrates how a small island can preserve evidence of interaction between different communities, with the sea acting as a route of exchange as well as a geographical boundary.

sections.title: Coastal forests in southern Somalia
sections.body: Bushbushle National Park lies in the Lower Juba region, part of the broader East African coastal forest environment. The area contains a mosaic of woodland and forest habitats influenced by seasonal rain and local terrain. It appears on Somalia's UNESCO Tentative List, not the inscribed World Heritage List. Its landscapes challenge the idea that the region can be described by a single arid habitat type.

sections.title: Ecology through changing seasons
sections.body: Rainfall patterns affect the growth of plants and availability of water. Some habitats may remain greener than nearby dry areas, allowing organisms to use a variety of ecological niches. Conservation requires scientific inventories and monitoring over time, especially where information is incomplete. The presence of forest does not guarantee that biodiversity will be protected without attention to surrounding land uses.

sections.title: Communities and the coastal region
sections.body: People in southern Somalia have long histories of farming, herding, fishing and exchange that vary with place. Describing a proposed protected landscape responsibly means recognising nearby livelihoods rather than presenting it as permanently uninhabited wilderness. Decisions over resources and access need to involve local communities and institutions as well as ecological specialists.

sections.title: Why tentative status matters
sections.body: UNESCO's Tentative List records properties proposed for possible future nomination; it is not confirmation of inscription or a complete scientific assessment. Bushbushle provides an opportunity to improve understanding of East African coastal ecosystems and how they relate to settlement and seasonal rainfall. Any release of this article should distinguish documented facts from conservation ambitions.

sections.title: A highland forest in Burundi
sections.body: Kibira National Park lies in north-western Burundi, where ridges and wetter upland environments support forest habitats. The park is on UNESCO's Tentative List, following a 2026 submission, but has not been inscribed on the World Heritage List. Its setting differs from the lowland environments often used to illustrate central and eastern Africa, with steep ground and contrasting microclimates.

sections.title: Plants, animals and water
sections.body: Montane forests support species adapted to cooler, wetter conditions at altitude. The vegetation also influences how rainfall reaches streams and soils, linking habitat health with downstream water systems. Biodiversity research is needed to monitor populations and understand ecological changes. A protected boundary alone does not stop all pressures reaching the forest from surrounding areas.

sections.title: Local relationships with forest
sections.body: Communities living near highland parks depend on land, agriculture and other resources. Conservation decisions can affect those activities, so governance and local participation are essential. The history of land use matters when interpreting the present-day forest. A description that celebrates biodiversity but overlooks people would be incomplete.

sections.title: A regional ecological connection
sections.body: Kibira forms part of a wider highland environment near the border with Rwanda. Maintaining ecological connections is important where forest remnants and human land uses meet. Studying the park provides a way to discuss how elevation, rainfall, species distribution and local livelihoods interact. Its tentative heritage status also demonstrates how countries research and document candidate sites before potential inscription.

sections.title: A huge landscape of seasonal movement
sections.body: Boma and Badingilo national parks and surrounding areas in South Sudan form a vast system of savanna, floodplain and wetland habitats. UNESCO inscribed the Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape on the World Heritage List in 2026. Rain and seasonal flooding alter the availability of food and water across the region, shaping the movement of animals and connections between habitats.

sections.title: Migration as an ecological process
sections.body: Large herds of antelope and gazelle move across extensive areas in response to seasonal conditions. Protecting them requires maintaining routes and habitats rather than conserving a single isolated point on a map. Predators, birds and smaller organisms also contribute to the wider ecosystem. Estimates of animal numbers require fieldwork, and conservation decisions depend on reliable monitoring.

sections.title: People living with changing seasons
sections.body: Diverse communities have long used the region for herding, farming and fishing, developing knowledge of local conditions. Their livelihoods interact with the same rainfall and flood patterns that influence wildlife. Successful management needs to recognise community interests, security and land-use decisions. The area should not be described as a wildlife landscape without people.

sections.title: A new international designation
sections.body: The 2026 inscription draws attention to ecological connectivity on an exceptional scale, while conservation challenges remain. Protecting such an extensive area involves research, management resources and cooperation across different landscapes. Boma–Badingilo is a striking example of how dynamic processes, rather than a single monument or dramatic viewpoint, can make a place internationally significant.

records.hook: Equatorial Guinea — Monte Alén National Park

sections.title: Forest on the mainland
sections.body: Monte Alén National Park lies in continental Equatorial Guinea, within the wider Central African forest region. Rivers, hills and tropical vegetation shape the landscape. In 2026 the country placed the park on its UNESCO Tentative List, meaning it is a candidate for possible future nomination rather than an inscribed World Heritage property. The area is an important example of habitats that are often less visible in international travel imagery.

sections.title: Biodiversity in layered habitats
sections.body: The forest contains different levels of vegetation and a range of ecological conditions. Birds, mammals, insects and plants use different parts of the environment, while waterways provide routes and habitat boundaries. Changes to land cover can affect animal movement and water quality. Scientific research helps establish which populations are present and how they respond to disturbance.

sections.title: Communities and conservation
sections.body: People near the park rely on land and natural resources in varied ways. Effective protection requires discussion of livelihoods and practical management with local authorities and communities. A designation cannot replace reliable monitoring or ensure that every ecological challenge has been resolved. The surrounding landscape can influence habitats inside the park.

sections.title: A place to study tropical forest
sections.body: Monte Alén makes it possible to examine the relationship between geology, rainfall, forest structure and wildlife in a Central African setting. Its relatively recent tentative-list submission also illustrates how national heritage initiatives are documented and discussed internationally. Presenting the site accurately means giving its current status and recognising that conservation is an ongoing process.

sections.title: Islands and tidal waters off West Africa
sections.body: The Bijagós Archipelago lies off Guinea-Bissau's Atlantic coast, where islands, sandbanks, mangroves and marine channels form a complex coastal system. UNESCO inscribed the Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago – Omatí Minhô in 2025. The protected property includes varied habitats rather than one island or a single stretch of beach.

sections.title: Animals linked by tides and seasons
sections.body: Coastal wetlands can support migrating birds, fish and other marine life. Mudflats change with the tide, making food and resting places available at different times. Marine habitats are linked through currents and animal movement, so environmental changes far from a particular island can matter. Research into species and water quality helps guide protection.

sections.title: Island communities and traditions
sections.body: People have lived in the archipelago for generations, shaping cultural landscapes and drawing on marine resources. Knowledge about seasons, fishing and local environments is part of understanding the islands. Conservation should not depict the archipelago as empty or overlook the role of communities in management. The surrounding coast also influences how islands connect with the mainland.

sections.title: Protection over a wide marine area
sections.body: The site's recent inscription reflects the importance of ecological processes across a network of islands and waters. Managing such a region requires attention to fishing, travel, habitat protection and local livelihoods. The Bijagós Archipelago shows that World Heritage recognition can concern living coastal ecosystems and their connections, not only famous buildings or landscapes.

sections.title: A wetland in a small Alpine state
sections.body: Ruggeller Riet lies in northern Liechtenstein near the Rhine valley. Its marshland vegetation and wet ground contrast with steep Alpine landscapes found elsewhere in the principality. The site is recognised under the international Ramsar Convention on Wetlands. This status is distinct from UNESCO World Heritage inscription, and its importance lies principally in ecological habitat and wetland conservation.

sections.title: Water creates specialised habitats
sections.body: Wetlands contain soils and plant communities influenced by water levels. Changes to drainage, rainfall or neighbouring land can alter those conditions and affect organisms that rely on them. Protecting a marsh requires more than retaining a patch of green on a map. Management must understand how water enters, moves through and leaves the site.

sections.title: A landscape shaped by nearby land use
sections.body: The Rhine valley contains farming, settlements and transport infrastructure, creating challenges for conserving wetland habitats. Historic drainage and other interventions changed parts of the landscape over time. Environmental managers must monitor vegetation and water conditions while considering surrounding communities. This connection between land use and ecology is especially visible in a small country with limited space.

sections.title: International recognition beyond UNESCO
sections.body: Ramsar designation is intended to support the conservation and wise use of wetlands. It should not be presented as a different spelling of World Heritage status. Ruggeller Riet is a useful example of how comparatively modest areas can be important for biodiversity and why protecting them may depend on decisions made outside their immediate boundaries.

records.focus: Ancient Capitals of the Kingdom of Tonga
records.hook: Tonga — Ancient Capitals of the Kingdom of Tonga

sections.title: Historic centres on Tongatapu
sections.body: The proposed Ancient Capitals of the Kingdom of Tonga property includes sites associated with earlier royal centres on Tongatapu. Monumental stone features and burial places preserve evidence of chiefly power, social organisation and skilled building. Tonga has placed these sites on UNESCO's Tentative List; they are not currently inscribed on the World Heritage List.

sections.title: Stone architecture and leadership
sections.body: The Ha'amonga 'a Maui trilithon is a prominent stone monument, while royal burial structures at Lapaha reflect different traditions of commemoration. Moving and shaping large coral-limestone blocks required planning and labour. Archaeology works alongside oral histories and genealogical traditions to investigate what these places meant. The different types of evidence do not always answer the same questions.

sections.title: A wider Pacific historical setting
sections.body: Tongan communities developed maritime connections with other Pacific islands, using sophisticated navigation and social networks. Historic capitals belonged to societies with agriculture, craft production and changing political relations. The monumental remains are only one aspect of life, and should not be treated as the entire history of Tonga or Oceania.

sections.title: Heritage with continuing meanings
sections.body: Some burial areas and traditions remain connected with present communities. Conservation must therefore respect cultural knowledge and the responsibilities of local custodians. These proposed sites show how archaeology and continuing social practices can contribute to understanding political history, while reminding visitors that a UNESCO Tentative List is a preliminary step rather than a final award.

records.hook: Monaco — Oceanographic Museum and marine science

sections.title: A museum overlooking the Mediterranean
sections.body: The Oceanographic Museum of Monaco stands above the Mediterranean coast and is associated with a long history of marine research and public education. Its collections and exhibitions explore sea life, ocean exploration and conservation. The museum is a cultural and scientific institution, not an independently inscribed UNESCO World Heritage property. Monaco's position on the coast gives its marine interests a strong geographical context.

sections.title: Research, specimens and observation
sections.body: Marine science depends on observing organisms and environments, from coastal habitats to deep water. Collections, aquariums and educational exhibits can make otherwise unfamiliar species accessible to visitors. They also raise important questions about responsible animal care, scientific evidence and the difference between preserved specimens and living ecosystems. No display can represent the full complexity of the Mediterranean Sea.

sections.title: A Mediterranean perspective
sections.body: Water movement, fisheries, tourism and urban development affect the coastline around Monaco and neighbouring countries. The sea connects their habitats and environmental pressures, making regional cooperation important. A museum can help explain these systems, but knowledge must be supported by continued research and data rather than only visually memorable exhibits.

sections.title: Science and public responsibility
sections.body: The institution provides a way to connect the history of oceanographic exploration with today's conservation challenges. Its role includes helping people understand habitats that may be distant or difficult to visit. The most valuable lesson is that understanding the ocean requires several approaches: measurement, ecology, careful communication and decisions about how people use marine environments.
